title: Explain functional animal anatomy and physiology

lessons.title: Homeostasis, temperature control and immunity
lessons.html:
Homeostasis

Functional anatomy looks at how body structures work together to keep the animal alive and productive. The central idea is homeostasis: the body keeps conditions such as temperature, blood sugar, water balance and blood pH within narrow limits. When stress pushes these out of balance, production falls first, then health.

Thermoregulation

Farm mammals and birds are warm-blooded. They balance heat produced by metabolism and rumen fermentation against heat lost to the environment.

  • Losing heat: sweating (good in cattle, poor in pigs and sheep), panting, blood flow to the skin, seeking shade and wallowing.
  • Conserving heat: shivering, hair standing up, huddling, reducing blood flow to the skin.

Heat stress in South African summers reduces feed intake, milk yield, sperm quality and conception rates. Zebu-type and Sanga cattle tolerate heat better thanks to a loose skin, short coat and more sweat glands. Management responses include shade, water close to the animals, cool-time handling and ventilation in sheds.

The immune system

The immune system defends the body against bacteria, viruses and parasites.

  • Non-specific defences: skin, mucus, stomach acid and white blood cells that engulf invaders.
  • Specific (acquired) immunity: lymphocytes produce antibodies against a particular organism and remember it.
TypeHow obtainedDuration
ActiveInfection or vaccination; body makes its own antibodiesLong-lasting, may need boosters
PassiveReady-made antibodies from colostrum or serumShort-term, fades over weeks

Ruminant placentas do not pass antibodies to the foetus, so newborn calves, lambs and kids depend entirely on colostrum. The gut can absorb these antibodies only for a short time after birth, which is why early colostrum intake is critical. Stress, malnutrition and heavy parasite loads all weaken immunity.

lessons.title: Digestive physiology of ruminants and monogastrics
lessons.html:
Rumen function

The rumen is a fermentation chamber kept at body temperature and a fairly stable pH. Billions of bacteria, protozoa and fungi break down cellulose that the animal's own enzymes cannot digest.

Products of fermentation

  • Volatile fatty acids (VFAs) - acetate, propionate and butyrate - are absorbed through the rumen wall and supply most of the ruminant's energy. Fibre-rich diets favour acetate, which supports milk fat; starch-rich diets favour propionate, which the liver turns into glucose.
  • Microbial protein - microbes use ammonia from protein and non-protein nitrogen to grow. They are washed into the abomasum and small intestine where they are digested, supplying high-quality protein.
  • Gases - carbon dioxide and methane are belched out. If belching is blocked, bloat results.

Rumination and saliva

Chewing the cud reduces particle size and stimulates large volumes of saliva, which contains bicarbonate that buffers rumen acid. Diets with too little effective fibre reduce rumination and saliva, so pH falls and acidosis follows. Monitoring the proportion of resting cows that are chewing the cud is a simple herd-level check.

The young ruminant

In a suckling calf the oesophageal groove closes when it drinks milk, directing milk past the rumen straight to the abomasum. The rumen develops as the calf eats dry feed; starter concentrates speed this up because VFAs stimulate growth of the rumen lining.

Monogastric digestion

In pigs and poultry, digestion relies on the animal's own enzymes. The stomach secretes acid and pepsin, the pancreas adds enzymes for starch, protein and fat, and the liver supplies bile for fat digestion. Most absorption happens in the small intestine through finger-like villi. Poultry have a crop for storage, a proventriculus (glandular stomach) and a muscular gizzard. Horses rely on caecum and colon fermentation, which is why sudden grain overload causes colic and laminitis.

lessons.title: Reproductive and lactation physiology
lessons.html:
Hormonal control of reproduction

Reproduction is controlled by hormones from the brain (hypothalamus and pituitary) and the gonads.

HormoneSourceMain action
FSHPituitaryStimulates follicle growth on the ovary
OestrogenGrowing follicleCauses heat signs and triggers the LH surge
LHPituitaryCauses ovulation and formation of the corpus luteum
ProgesteroneCorpus luteum, later placentaMaintains pregnancy; blocks new heats
Prostaglandin F2-alphaUterusDestroys the corpus luteum if no pregnancy, so the cycle restarts
TestosteroneTestesSperm production, male behaviour and libido

These hormones explain synchronisation programmes. Products containing progesterone or prostaglandin are used under veterinary guidance to bring groups of females into heat together for artificial insemination. Because prostaglandin can end a pregnancy, these products must only be used as prescribed. Pregnant women should not handle them, as the label warns.

Seasonal breeding

Some species respond to day length. Many sheep and goat breeds cycle more strongly as days shorten in autumn, controlled by the hormone melatonin. Horses are long-day breeders. Cattle and pigs breed all year if well fed.

Lactation physiology

  • The udder is made of milk-producing alveoli, ducts, gland and teat cisterns, and the teat canal with its sphincter muscle.
  • Prolactin supports milk synthesis.
  • Oxytocin, released when the teats are stimulated or the cow hears the routine, contracts cells around the alveoli and causes let-down for a few minutes.
  • Adrenaline, released when animals are frightened or hurt, blocks oxytocin, so rough handling reduces yield.

The teat canal and its keratin plug are the main barrier against mastitis bacteria. After milking the canal stays open for a while, which is why post-dipping and keeping cows standing help.

Key points

  • Homeostasis keeps temperature, water and chemistry within limits; stress breaks it.
  • Newborn ruminants get passive immunity only from colostrum.
  • Rumen VFAs supply most ruminant energy; saliva buffers rumen acid.
  • FSH, oestrogen, LH, progesterone and prostaglandin control the oestrous cycle.
  • Oxytocin causes milk let-down; adrenaline from stress blocks it.
